name: Spinocerebellar ataxia type 23 (PDYN)
aliases: autosomal dominant cerebellar ataxia type SCA23

clinicalPearls: A rare autosomal dominant cerebellar ataxia caused by missense variants in PDYN, which encodes prodynorphin, the precursor of the opioid peptide dynorphin
Presentation is usually in adulthood, often mid-to-late, with slowly progressive gait ataxia and dysarthria

Alongside cerebellar signs, posterior-column sensory features such as reduced vibration and joint-position sense may be present, together with pyramidal signs like hyperreflexia and extensor plantar responses
Eye-movement abnormalities including gaze-evoked nystagmus and abnormal saccades are described
Because it is caused by point mutations, repeat-expansion testing is normal and diagnosis relies on gene sequencing
Brain MRI shows cerebellar atrophy, sometimes with brainstem involvement
There is no specific therapy; care is supportive and multidisciplinary
reference.pathophysiology: SCA23 is caused by dominant missense variants in PDYN, which encodes prodynorphin, a precursor processed into dynorphin peptides that act on kappa-opioid receptors and modulate neurotransmission. Pathogenic variants tend to cluster in the region giving rise to dynorphin A and are thought to yield abnormally stable or neurotoxic peptides that disturb glutamatergic signalling and neuronal calcium handling. The consequent Purkinje cell and related neuronal degeneration produces the cerebellar ataxia, with variable posterior-column and pyramidal involvement reflecting wider effects on neuronal survival.
additionalDifferentials: Friedreich ataxia and other ataxias with posterior-column involvement
Subacute combined degeneration from vitamin B12 deficiency
additionalInvestigations: PDYN sequencing within an ataxia gene panel or exome
Brain MRI to document cerebellar and any brainstem atrophy
Testing for common repeat-expansion SCAs before proceeding to PDYN analysis
Nerve conduction studies and vitamin B12 and E levels where posterior-column signs are present
Detailed family history to establish autosomal dominant transmission
Screening for acquired ataxia (thyroid function, coeliac serology, alcohol history)
redFlags: Rapid progression or an atypical course suggesting an acquired or paraneoplastic cause
Prominent autonomic failure pointing to multiple system atrophy
Severe sensory ataxia disproportionate to cerebellar signs, prompting a search for a treatable neuropathy
Dysphagia with aspiration risk requiring swallow assessment
reference.prognosis: SCA23 is slowly progressive over years, with gradually increasing gait and speech difficulty; disability varies between families and life expectancy is often relatively preserved, prognosis being influenced by bulbar involvement and falls.
pitfalls: Expecting a repeat expansion and missing the point mutation when common panels are negative
Attributing posterior-column sensory signs to an acquired neuropathy without pursuing a genetic cause
Not proceeding to sequencing when the phenotype fits a rare dominant ataxia
Overlooking multiple system atrophy when autonomic features are present
Failing to offer genetic counselling regarding dominant inheritance
references: Bradley and Daroff's Neurology in Clinical Practice
management: With no disease-modifying therapy for this PDYN-related ataxia, base care on physiotherapy for gait and balance, occupational therapy, and speech and language therapy for dysarthria
Manage pyramidal spasticity with physiotherapy, stretching and an antispasticity agent such as baclofen
Address posterior-column sensory ataxia with proprioceptive rehabilitation, walking aids and falls prevention
Exclude and treat modifiable causes of posterior-column signs, notably vitamin B12 and vitamin E deficiency
Monitor for bulbar involvement with periodic swallow assessment, as this influences prognosis
Offer genetic counselling and cascade testing for the autosomal dominant transmission
